I need something practical enough to brief nontechnical board members before we decide whether nuclear supply risk is a deal-breaker or just a manageable procurement issue.

The short answer is that uranium supply risk is real, but it is not one single “uranium” risk and should not be treated exactly like a gas-supply crisis.  
For a conventional reactor, the board should separate four exposures: mined uranium, conversion into uranium hexafluoride, enrichment, and fuel fabrication. [shard_05269_31146] [shard_06007_29187]

Mining is geographically concentrated, with Kazakhstan historically supplying roughly 45% of world uranium and Kazakhstan, Canada, and Australia among the leading producers. [shard_05238_48417] [shard_00602_83033]  
Kazakhstan concentration is important, but it does not mean that a Kazakh uranium contract is automatically a Russian-free fuel contract, because Kazakhstan’s conversion, enrichment, and much of its fuel-assembly chain have historically been outside the country, including in Russia. [shard_02369_46810]  
Kazatomprom’s position is also vulnerable to non-geological constraints such as production limits and shortages of inputs including sulphuric acid, while industry forecasts cited in the corpus point to possible future supply deficits. [shard_06516_69556]

The mining risk is mainly a long-cycle availability and price risk: years of weak exploration and mine-development spending, radioactive-material regulation, and high-cost capacity make production slow to respond when demand rises. [shard_00950_26981]  
That means a utility can face a tight market years before the reactor actually runs short of fuel, because it may have to compete for future production or pay more to secure conversion, enrichment, or fabrication capacity. [shard_00950_26981] [shard_01868_5915]

The Russia exposure is more serious in midstream services than the mine-origin map alone suggests.  
The cited supply-chain evidence attributes approximately one-third of 2020 conversion supply and 43% of global enrichment capacity to Russia, with additional capacity in Europe, China, and the United States. [shard_04912_28668]  
Russia has also used integrated fuel-cycle offerings and long-term enrichment contracts with utilities, so a contract can be legally long-term while still leaving the buyer exposed to Russian processing, transport, sanctions, or export-policy risk. [shard_03247_71868] [shard_04912_28668]

China matters less as a simple source of mined uranium in this evidence than as an expanding conversion, enrichment, and advanced-fuel competitor, with China identified alongside Russia as having the infrastructure to produce HALEU at scale in the period described. [shard_05037_47072] [shard_04912_28668]  
Stockpiles, depleted uranium that can be re-enriched, recycled material, and former weapons material provide buffers, but those buffers are not a guaranteed substitute for continuing commercial production and can change abruptly when government policy changes. [shard_05280_38960] [shard_05238_48417]

Price risk is therefore broader than the uranium spot price.  
The spot market is only a small part of consumption, while most utility purchasing occurs through longer-term arrangements, and reported conversion and enrichment prices have also risen sharply. [shard_01504_57750]  
Long-term price indicators are intended to represent multi-year, production-based supply beginning several years ahead, so they are better viewed as signals of the cost of securing future capacity than as a simple hedge against tomorrow’s spot price. [shard_01868_5915]  
A long-term contract can reduce exposure to short-term price spikes and improve delivery priority, but it does not eliminate price escalation, supplier credit risk, sanctions risk, transport disruption, or the possibility that a supplier lacks the contracted material. [shard_01868_5915] [shard_03242_80346]

The board should insist that a proposed power-purchase agreement identify not merely the uranium miner but the actual origin, owner, and reserved capacity for conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication, transport, and finished assemblies. [shard_05269_31146] [shard_06007_29187]  
It should require more than one qualified source for each separable stage, explicit limits on Russian and other politically unacceptable content, rights to substitute suppliers, and enough lead time to qualify replacement fuel. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_03242_80346]  
Commercial protections should include firm delivery obligations, supplier financial security, inventory or borrowing rights, transparent escalation formulas, caps or reopeners for extreme price movements, force-majeure limits, and compensation if replacement purchases are required. [shard_01868_5915] [shard_04029_80802]  
The utility should also maintain a strategic inventory or assured access to inventory where licensing and operating rules permit, because mines supplied only about 77% of utilities’ annual uranium requirements in the cited 2021 data and the balance came from stockpiles. [shard_05238_48417]

A future advanced SMR creates a different and potentially sharper risk because many designs require HALEU, uranium enriched above 5% and up to 20%, rather than the roughly 5%-or-less fuel used by the existing fleet. [shard_04225_54023] [shard_02508_35653]  
The evidence describes HALEU as not yet widely commercially available, with Russia and China possessing scale infrastructure, a US producer reaching only demonstration-scale output in October 2023, and new requirements for enrichment cascades, transport containers, fabrication, licensing, and substantial capital. [shard_05037_47072]  
Consequently, an SMR option should not be treated as protected merely because its vendor promises to supply fuel; the board should require a credible, funded HALEU production and fabrication pathway, named backup suppliers, delivery milestones, and a remedy if the fuel supply is unavailable. [shard_05037_47072] [shard_02108_21092]

My practical classification would be “manageable procurement risk” for a conventional reactor only if the PPA includes genuine multi-stage fuel assurance and diversification, but “material project risk” for an advanced SMR until its HALEU supply chain is demonstrated and contractually backstopped. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_05037_47072]  
The deal becomes a potential red flag if it relies on one miner, one converter or enricher, Russian-linked processing, an uncapped spot-price fallback, or an SMR fuel promise that depends on infrastructure still awaiting construction. [shard_02369_46810] [shard_04912_28668] [shard_05037_47072]
